extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, regulatory toxicologists, and SDS/hazard classifiers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for classifying substances and mixtures for serious eye damage/eye irritation, respiratory and skin sensitization, germ cell mutagenicity, and carcinogenicity, including concentration cut-offs, bridging principles, and evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered approach to testing mixtures for eye damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical manufacturers shall use a tiered approach as included in the criteria for classification of substances for skin corrosion and serious eye damage and eye irritation to help ensure an accurate classification, as well as to avoid unnecessary animal testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of any other information, a mixture is considered to cause serious eye damage (Category 1) if it has a pH ≤2 or ≥11.5. However, if consideration of acid/alkaline reserve suggests the mixture may not have the potential to cause serious eye damage despite the low or high pH value, then further evaluation may be necessary. Apply tiered weight-of-evidence steps and avoid animal testing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principles when mixture itself not tested
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the mixture itself has not been tested to determine its hazard, but there are sufficient data on individual ingredients and similar tested mixtures to adequately characterize hazards, these data will be used in accordance with the bridging principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreed bridging principles include: Dilution, Batching, Concentration of mixtures, Interpolation within one hazard category (or subcategory), Substantially similar mixtures, and Aerosols (see paragraph A.0.5). Use bridging to infer mixture classification from ingredient and analogous-mixture data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of relevant ingredients for mixture classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The “relevant ingredients” of a mixture are those which are present in concentrations ≥1% (w/w for solids/liquids/dusts/mists/vapors; v/v for gases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the classifier has reason to suspect that an ingredient present at a concentration <1% will affect classification of the mixture for serious eye damage/eye irritation, that ingredient shall also be considered relevant. This definition is used when applying additivity and cut-off rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity approach for mixtures (eye damage/irritation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When data are available on ingredients but not on the mixture, classification is based on the theory of additivity: each corrosive or eye-damaging/irritant ingredient contributes in proportion to its potency and concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weighting factor of 10 is used for skin corrosive and serious eye damaging ingredients when present below the concentration limit for Category 1 but at concentrations that will contribute to classification. The mixture is classified when the sum of concentrations (accounting for weighting) exceeds threshold cut-off values (see Table A.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cut-off values/concentration limits (Table A.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the cut-off value/concentration limits in Table A.3.3 to determine if a mixture must be classified as seriously damaging to the eye or an eye irritant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.3.3 specifies the concentration sums (and combinations of ingredient categories) that trigger classification of the mixture as Serious eye damage (Category 1) or Eye irritation (Category 2/2A/2B). Note-specific rules: an ingredient classified as both skin Category 1 and eye Category 1 is counted only once; mixtures where all relevant ingredients are Eye Irritation Category 2B may be classified Category 2B. Apply the table values and notes when performing calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules when additivity approach does not apply (Table A.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain chemicals (e.g., acids and bases, inorganic salts, aldehydes, phenols, surfactants) the additivity approach may not work and special cut-offs apply as summarized in Table A.3.4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Table A.3.4: Acid with pH <2 at ≥1% → Serious eye damage (Category 1); Base with pH ≥11.5 at ≥1% → Serious eye damage (Category 1); Other skin corrosive or serious eye damage (Category 1) ingredients at ≥1% → Category 1; Other eye irritant (Category 2) ingredients at ≥3% → Eye irritation (Category 2). For mixtures containing strong acids/bases, pH (with consideration of acid/alkali reserve) is a better indicator than concentration limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: When reliable ingredient/mixture data override generic cut-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: On occasion, reliable data may show that the (irreversible/reversible) eye effects of an ingredient will not be evident when present at a level above the generic cut-off values/concentration limits; in these cases the mixture could be classified according to those data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If expected effects will not be evident despite ingredient concentrations above generic cut-offs, testing of the mixture may be considered. Apply the tiered weight-of-evidence approach (section A.3.2, Figure A.3.1) and ensure mixture test results are conclusive with respect to dose, duration, observations, and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredient-specific low-concentration considerations (eye/skin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are data showing that ingredient(s) may be corrosive to the skin or seriously damaging to the eye/eye irritating at concentrations ≤1% (corrosive/serious eye damage) or ≤3% (eye irritant), the mixture shall be classified accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to paragraph A.0.4.3 on use of cut-off values/concentration limits. Such ingredient-specific evidence can mandate mixture classification even when generic additivity thresholds are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiratory sensitizer classification — weight of evidence and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances may be allocated to sub-categories 1A or 1B using a weight of evidence approach based on reliable and good quality evidence from human cases/epidemiology and/or appropriate animal studies; where data are insufficient for sub-categorization, classify as Category 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1A: high frequency of occurrence in humans or high probability based on tests; Category 1B: low-to-moderate frequency or probability. Severity of reaction may also be considered. Use weight-of-evidence evaluation per Table A.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evidence requirements for respiratory sensitizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a substance can lead to specific respiratory hypersensitivity is normally based on human experience (e.g., asthma, rhinitis/conjunctivitis, alveolitis) and need not demonstrate immunological mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering human evidence, also consider (a) size of the population exposed and (b) extent of exposure. Evidence can include clinical history, lung function tests related to exposure, in vivo/in vitro immunological tests (e.g., skin prick, serology), studies indicating hypersensitivity reactions, a chemical structure related to known respiratory sensitizers, and positive bronchial challenge tests conducted per accepted guidelines (positive challenge tests may be sufficient on their own). Clinical history should include medical and occupational histories, aggravating factors, onset/progression, family history, other allergic disorders, and smoking history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal evidence for respiratory sensitizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Data from appropriate animal studies indicative of inhalation sensitization in humans may be considered in classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include measurements of IgE and other immunological parameters in mice and specific pulmonary responses in guinea pigs. Use these animal data in a weight-of-evidence approach alongside human evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin sensitizer classification — categories and weight-of-evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects seen in humans or animals normally justify classification in a weight-of-evidence approach for skin sensitizers. Substances may be allocated to sub-categories 1A or 1B using the criteria in Table A.4.2; if data are insufficient for sub-categorization, classify in Category 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1A: high frequency in humans and/or high potency in animals; Category 1B: low-to-moderate frequency/potency. Severity of reaction may be considered. Follow guidance values for sub-categorization in subsequent paragraphs and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evidence thresholds for skin sensitizer subcategories
rubrics_metrics.description: Human evidence for sub-category 1A may include positive responses at ≤500 μg/cm2 in HRIPT or HMT induction threshold; sub-category 1B may include positive responses at >500 μg/cm2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider diagnostic patch test data showing relatively high (1A) or low but substantial (1B) incidence in a defined population relative to exposure, and epidemiological evidence of incidence relative to exposure. Use these thresholds when interpreting human patch-test/epidemiological data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal test criteria for skin sensitizers (LLNA, guinea pig, Buehler)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Category 1, adjuvant-type tests: ≥30% of animals considered positive; non-adjuvant guinea pig test: ≥15% positive; in LLNA a stimulation index (SI) ≥3 is positive. Specific numeric criteria for sub-categories are provided (EC3 values and percentage responding thresholds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.4.3 (sub-category 1A) example: LLNA EC3 ≤2%; guinea pig maximization ≥30% responding at ≤0.1% induction dose or ≥60% responding at >0.1% to ≤1%; Buehler ≥15% responding at ≤0.2% topical induction dose or ≥60% responding at >0.2% to ≤20%. Table A.4.4 (sub-category 1B) gives the corresponding less potent thresholds (e.g., EC3 >2%). Use these assay-specific thresholds when assigning sub-categories from animal data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific considerations and weight-of-evidence rules for skin sensitization
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence for classification should include one or more of: positive patch testing (normally from >1 clinic), epidemiological studies showing allergic contact dermatitis, positive animal studies, positive experimental human studies, well-documented episodes from multiple clinics, and severity of reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When human and animal data conflict, assess quality and reliability to resolve classification case-by-case; human data often come from less controlled sources and should be evaluated cautiously. Negative human data should not normally negate positive animal results. A combination of two or more weaker indicators (e.g., isolated episodes, limited epidemiology, near-threshold animal tests, non-standard methods, positive close structural analogues) may alter the decision and should be considered case-by-case. Immunological contact urticaria may lead to skin sensitizer classification, based primarily on human evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification for sensitizers — cut-off values (Table A.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixture shall be classified as a respiratory or skin sensitizer when at least one ingredient has been classified as such and is present at or above the cut-off/concentration limits shown in Table A.4.5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Table A.4.5: Respiratory Sensitizer Category 1 (all physical states) cut-off ≥0.1%; Respiratory Sensitizer Sub-category 1B cut-off ≥1.0% for solids/liquids and ≥0.2% for gases; Skin Sensitizer Category 1 and Sub-category 1A cut-off ≥0.1% (solids/liquids); Skin Sensitizer Sub-category 1B cut-off ≥1.0%. Apply state-specific gas/solid-liquid distinctions where noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Germ cell mutagenicity categories and evidence basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification system provides for two categories of germ cell mutagens: Category 1 (1A and 1B) for substances known or regarded as if they induce heritable mutations in germ cells, and Category 2 for substances causing concern based on evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1A: positive evidence from human epidemiological studies. Category 1B: positive results from in vivo heritable germ cell mutagenicity tests in mammals or in vivo somatic cell mutagenicity plus supporting evidence of germ cell effects. Category 2: positive mammalian experiments and/or supported in vitro evidence. Classification is hazard-based and uses weight-of-evidence and expert judgment; consider route relevance and test validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification for germ cell mutagens — cut-off values (Table A.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of mixtures shall be based on ingredient test data using cut-off values/concentration limits for ingredients classified as germ cell mutagens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.5.1: Ingredient classified as Category 1A/B mutagen → mixture classification triggered at ≥0.1%; Category 2 mutagen → mixture classification triggered at ≥1.0%. Cut-offs apply to solids/liquids (w/w) and gases (v/v). Mixture-level test data may modify classification on a case-by-case basis if conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of scientifically validated mutagenicity/genotoxicity test methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists example validated assays for in vivo heritable germ cell mutagenicity, in vivo somatic cell mutagenicity, mutagenicity/genotoxicity in germ and somatic cells, and in vitro tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include OECD methods: Rodent dominant lethal mutation test (OECD 478), Mouse heritable translocation assay (OECD 485), mammalian bone marrow chromosome aberration test (OECD 475), mammalian erythrocyte micronucleus test (OECD 474), in vitro mammalian chromosome aberration (OECD 473), in vitro mammalian cell gene mutation (OECD 476), bacterial reverse mutation (OECD 471). New validated tests may also be used in the overall weight of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carcinogenicity classification — categories and strength-of-evidence approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances are allocated to Category 1 (1A or 1B) or Category 2 based on strength of evidence and additional weight-of-evidence considerations; classification is hazard-based and intended to reflect intrinsic carcinogenic potential, not quantitative risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1A: known human carcinogens (largely human evidence). Category 1B: presumed human carcinogens (largely animal evidence). Category 2: suspected human carcinogens (limited human and/or animal evidence). Classification is a one-step criterion-based process involving evaluation of strength of evidence and consideration of other relevant information (weight of evidence). Use IARC and other guidance for interpreting 'sufficient' vs 'limited' evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in carcinogenicity weight-of-evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of factors should be considered that influence the overall likelihood that an agent may pose a carcinogenic hazard in humans beyond tumor enumeration and statistical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important factors include: tumor type and background incidence; multisite responses; progression of lesions to malignancy; reduced tumor latency; whether responses are in single/both sexes; single or several species; structural similarity to known carcinogens; routes of exposure; comparison of ADME between animals and humans; potential confounding by excessive toxicity at test doses; mode of action and its human relevance (e.g., mutagenicity, cytotoxicity with growth stimulation, mitogenesis, immunosuppression). Evidence of mutagenic activity in vivo may indicate carcinogenic potential. Consider structural analogues and metabolite formation where direct data are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture classification for carcinogens — cut-off values and SDS requirement (Table A.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixture shall be classified as a carcinogen when at least one ingredient has been classified as Category 1 or Category 2 carcinogen and is present at or above the cut-off values shown in Table A.6.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.6.1: Category 1 carcinogen ingredient → mixture trigger at ≥0.1%; Category 2 carcinogen ingredient → trigger at ≥0.1% (note: if Category 2 ingredient is present between 0.1% and 1%, information is required on the SDS for the product). Apply these cut-offs when determining mixture labeling and SDS content.
